hook: You know about turning the other cheek. But did you know Jesus names the right cheek, and that a blow there was a special kind of insult?
known: Often quoted as advice to let people walk over you.
who: Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount.
audience: His disciples, with the crowds listening (Matthew 5:1-2).
setting: The fifth of six places in this chapter where Jesus quotes what his hearers had been taught and then says what he himself requires. Here the saying is “An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth”.
around: The rule he quotes comes from the law of Moses, where it tells judges to match the penalty to the harm (Exodus 21:23-25). Jesus answers it with four pictures from daily life: a blow to the cheek, a lawsuit over a coat, being compelled to go a mile, and a request for a loan. Then he goes further still: “love your enemies”.
point: Jesus forbids hitting back, and the detail of the right cheek suggests he has insult in view as much as injury. How far the command reaches is read differently among Christians. The article on this site about turning the other cheek sets those readings side by side.
story:
Jesus says the right cheek. Most people are right-handed, and a right hand reaches another person’s right cheek most easily with its back. Scholars have long noticed the detail. Jewish law written down some generations later shows why it matters: the Mishnah sets the fine for a slap at two hundred dinars, and for a slap with the back of the hand at four hundred. The backhand was the more degrading blow.

So Jesus is probably not picturing a fight. He is picturing a humiliation.

The writer Walter Wink built a well-known reading on this. A backhand, he said, was how a master put a slave back in his place. Whoever turns the other cheek refuses that place. Without hitting back, the gesture says: I am not beneath you.

Many readers find this convincing. Other scholars are more careful. Some read the saying simply as a ban on paying back in kind, and some warn against finding one fixed strategy in it. Either way the sentence carried a weight in its own time that is easy to miss now.

sources.title: Walter Wink, Nonviolence for the Violent, lecture transcript (Lutheran Peace Fellowship)
